rv.q: We've all seen the scene in "A Christmas Story" when the kid gets his tongue stuck on a frozen flagpole. Now on Broadway is that very same scene – plus the kid actually singing through it, or at least trying to sing. "Sthlun luv a...," he mumbles at the end.
The musical adaptation manages to capture much of the charm and humor of the classic holiday film, with strong performances and clever staging.
In this case, perseverance — and a willingness by producers to identify problems and make necessary changes — has paid off in a merry way indeed.
A Christmas Story is what happens when rare respect for source material meets utter sincerity and unimpeachable talent.
A cut above the pack, it's cute, corny, wholesome and sentimental – all basic requirements for family-friendly seasonal stage entertainment.
The charming musical that opened last night on Broadway succeeds both as an adaptation and on its own terms.
The show is sweet without being saccharine, funny without being crude, and it captures the essential spirit of Jean Shepherd's beloved story without dumbing it down.

In fact, not much is sacred in this droll, imaginative, definitely and a bit defiantly off-center tale of a 9-year-old bespectacled kid named Ralphie and a flawed but loving family in Indiana in the 1940s.
You'd have to have a Grinch-size heart not to feel a smile spreading across your face when Luke Spring starts tapping his little heart out.
But when all the wrapping and bows come off, you'll be disappointed to find a sweater where you really wanted a gun.
The show feels too long, particularly in the first act.
A Christmas Story succeeds as well as it does because it doesn't try to be anything more than what it is: a gentle, sweet, and ultimately satisfying look at one boy's holiday dreams.
A The Musical is a sweet, nostalgic trip down memory lane that captures the essence of the beloved film while adding its own theatrical magic.
A Christmas Story: The Musical is a sweet, nostalgic show that captures the spirit of the beloved 1983 movie without being slavishly devoted to it.
